pages.text: The autumn market was nearly empty. The sun hung low and golden, and the air smelled of figs and warm bread. At the pomegranate stall, Sofia and Liam were helping out. The seller had the biggest laugh in the whole market.
pages.speech: The autumn market was nearly empty. The sun hung low and golden, and the air smelled of figs and warm bread. At the pomegranate stall, Sofia and Liam were helping out. The seller had the biggest laugh in the whole market.

pages.text: Only ten pomegranates were left on the table, round and red and shiny. Liam counted them, tapping each one with his finger. “Ten,” he said. Sofia brought two empty baskets from behind the crates.

pages.text: “Two customers are coming,” said the seller. “The baker wants some, and the doctor wants some. Can you share them out for me?” Then she went to stack the empty crates at the back. Her laugh rolled all the way down the row.
pages.speech: “Two customers are coming,” said the seller. “The baker wants some, and the doctor wants some. Can you share them out for me?” Then she went to stack the empty crates at the back. Her laugh rolled all the way down the row.

pages.text: “Easy,” said Liam. “Five for the baker and five for the doctor. That’s fair.” They counted them in together: one, two, three, four, five, and one, two, three, four, five. Two baskets, exactly the same. Liam folded his arms. Job done.

pages.text: But then the baker came hurrying down the row, with flour on his apron and flour in his eyebrows. “Seven!” he puffed. “I need seven pomegranates for my juice.” Liam looked at his neat baskets. “But we made them fair,” he said.
pages.speech: But then the baker came hurrying down the row, with flour on his apron and flour in his eyebrows. “Seven!” he puffed. “I need seven pomegranates for my juice.” Liam looked at his neat baskets. “But we made them fair,” he said.

pages.text: Sofia thought for a moment. Then she took one pomegranate from the doctor’s basket and put it in the baker’s. Then one more. “Seven for you,” she said, “and three for the doctor.” Liam counted everything again, slowly. “Seven and three,” he said. “Still ten.” He sounded surprised.
pages.speech: Sofia thought for a moment. Then she took one pomegranate from the doctor’s basket and put it in the baker’s. Then one more. “Seven for you,” she said, “and three for the doctor.” Liam counted everything again, slowly. “Seven and three,” he said. “Still ten.” He sounded surprised.

pages.text: Just then the doctor arrived, holding a small bag in both hands. “Only two for me today, please,” she said softly. “My bag is very small.” Sofia lifted one pomegranate out of the doctor’s basket and put it down on the table. Two left in the basket. Good.
pages.speech: Just then the doctor arrived, holding a small bag in both hands. “Only two for me today, please,” she said softly. “My bag is very small.” Sofia lifted one pomegranate out of the doctor’s basket and put it down on the table. Two left in the basket. Good.

pages.text: Liam wanted to be sure. He counted the baker’s basket: seven. He counted the doctor’s basket: two. “Seven and two make nine,” he said slowly. His tummy gave a jump. “Nine? We had ten. We’ve lost one!”
pages.speech: Liam wanted to be sure. He counted the baker’s basket: seven. He counted the doctor’s basket: two. “Seven and two make nine,” he said slowly. His tummy gave a jump. “Nine? We had ten. We’ve lost one!”

pages.text: Everybody started looking. Sofia looked in the empty crates. The baker looked behind the sacks. The doctor looked inside her small bag. Even the seller stopped laughing and looked in her apron pocket. There was no pomegranate anywhere.
pages.speech: Everybody started looking. Sofia looked in the empty crates. The baker looked behind the sacks. The doctor looked inside her small bag. Even the seller stopped laughing and looked in her apron pocket. There was no pomegranate anywhere.

pages.text: Then Sofia saw it, and she started to giggle. The lost pomegranate was in Liam’s own hand. He had picked it up off the table while he was counting. He had been holding it all along. Liam stared at it. Then everybody laughed, and the seller laughed loudest of all.

pages.text: “Seven, and two, and one in my hand,” said Liam. “That makes ten again.” The baker grinned. “Then give me that one too,” he said. “I’ll take eight.” Into his basket it went. Eight for the baker, two for the doctor. Ten.

pages.text: Sofia pushed the two baskets side by side. “Five and five. Seven and three. Eight and two,” she said, tapping each basket. “However we share them, it always makes ten.” Liam’s eyes lit up. “What about nine and one?” he asked. He moved one pomegranate across to try it. “Not my two!” laughed the doctor, so he quickly moved it back.

pages.text: The baker paid and hurried off with eight pomegranates for his juice. The doctor paid and walked away with two in her small bag. Both of them waved. Now the baskets were empty, and the table was empty too.

pages.text: The seller came back, wiping her hands on her apron. “Well done, my helpers,” she said. Then she reached under the table and brought out one more pomegranate, wrapped in a cloth. Its skin had split open, as very ripe pomegranates sometimes do. “This one I never sell,” she said. “This one is for us.”
pages.speech: The seller came back, wiping her hands on her apron. “Well done, my helpers,” she said. Then she reached under the table and brought out one more pomegranate, wrapped in a cloth. Its skin had split open, as very ripe pomegranates sometimes do. “This one I never sell,” she said. “This one is for us.”

pages.text: She broke it open with her thumbs. Inside, the seeds shone like tiny red lamps. Liam leaned in close. “How many seeds are there?” he asked. The seller laughed her biggest laugh of all. “More than ten,” she said. “Much, much more than ten.” And they ate them together, one shining seed at a time.

activity.title: Bowling with Ten
activity.goal: Add two scores together to find the total.
materials: Ten cardboard tubes (kitchen-roll or toilet-roll tubes)

steps.caption: Stand ten tubes in a triangle.
Roll the ball. Low and slow.
How many fell? How many stand?

activity.safety: Use a soft ball and roll it along the floor; never throw it. Play in a clear space, away from glass, stairs and sharp furniture corners. Nobody stands in the lane while the ball is rolling. Emergency: 101 in Israel, 112 in Denmark.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Sofia and Liam discover that however you share ten pomegranates between two baskets, the two parts always make ten. This game turns that discovery into something your child can do with their whole body, and adds the activity’s own goal: adding two scores to find a total. Collect ten cardboard tubes over a week or two (kitchen-roll or toilet-roll tubes; if you cut long tubes shorter, the adult does the cutting). Stand them in a triangle at the end of a clear hallway: one at the front, then two, three and four. Mark a rolling line two or three metres away with a shoe or a strip of tape. Your child kneels at the line and rolls the soft ball along the floor. Before counting, ask them to guess: ‘Three fell down. How many do you think are still standing?’ Then count to check. Fallen and standing always make ten, just like the baskets in the story, and children love testing it again and again. The number that fell is the score: your child writes it on the score sheet (here, digits are fine). Stand the tubes up and play a second round. Then add the two scores: ‘Four in the first round and six in the second. How many altogether?’ Let them count on their fingers or draw dots; there is no rush. Praise the effort and the careful counting (‘you checked it twice’), not being ‘clever’. Twenty to thirty minutes is about right. To make it easier, use five tubes, or roll from closer. To make it harder, play three rounds, aim to reach exactly twenty, or write each roll as a number sentence, such as 3 + 7 = 10.
activity.inClass: Teams of four, each with its own lane in a corridor or the playground and its own ten tubes. Give each child a job and swap jobs every turn: one rolls, one stands the tubes back up, one counts the fallen and standing tubes out loud, and one keeps the score sheet. At the end, each child adds their two scores. The teacher walks from lane to lane asking ‘How many fell? So how many are still standing?’
